transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-01 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Ruth (Redwood), Aisha (BlueHarbor), Luca (BlueHarbor), Priya (BlueHarbor), Marco (BlueHarbor)

Summary:
High-level technical deep dive focused on throughput tradeoffs for BlueHarbor's on-prem inference cluster. Topics: continuous batching behavior with bursty traffic, configuring prefetch/window sizes, max_num_seqs (max sequences per GPU), token floors/ceil guards, KV cache prewarm and eviction, quantization implications (int8/int4) on latency vs throughput, network/VPC constraints. Agreed next steps include sharing knob spreadsheet, traffic histograms, and scheduling a pilot run.

Topics:
- continuous batching and scheduler governor behavior
- prefetch window vs token-floor interaction
- max_num_seqs and token guard tuning for finance workloads
- KV cache hit-rate tradeoffs and prewarm strategies
- quantization impact on token latency tail (int8 vs int4)
- on-prem networking and KMS considerations

Action items (see metadata): Jonas to produce spreadsheet; Aisha to share histograms; Maya to schedule pilot; Priya to confirm security constraints.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay, thanks everyone for joining. think we'll jump right in, uh this is the throughput tuning deep dive for the on prem cluster, BlueHarbor. Jonas is gonna lead the knobs discussion.
[00:22] Jonas: hey all. quick context check, Aisha — when you say peak RPS you were talking 1200 concurrent requests or 1.2k per second?
[00:35] Aisha: yeah more like bursts to 1.2k rps but they are short, like 20 to 90 seconds and then drop to a few hundred. our median is much lower. also seq lengths vary — most requests 60-120 tokens but some go to 800 tokens for long document summarization.
[00:52] Jonas: okay that distribution matters a lot for max_num_seqs. if you've got many long sequences then packing helps but it reduces the number of parallel seqs we can host per GPU.
[01:13] Luca: quick q — we are on nv4-like GPUs and plan to run quantized models, int8 mostly, may test int4 for cheaper throughput. any real-world gotchas?
[01:25] Jonas: int8 tends to be sweet spot; int4 can reduce memory but sometimes increases compute path variance and can spike latency tail, especially with longer sequences. also kv cache sizes change, so prefetching and eviction settings need adjustments.
[01:44] Marco: our infra constraint is that we can't open wide egress to the public cloud, so on-prem must do all model inference; we will have KMS in our VPC.
[01:55] Ruth: noted — we'll run through KMS and network checklist later in the call.

[02:10] Jonas: alright, i'll sketch the knob set. primary knobs: continuous_batch_window (ms), max_num_seqs, token_floor (min tokens to batch), token_ceil / per-request token limit, slot_size (in tokens), prefetch_window (how far ahead we warm KV), eviction_policy / kvcache_hitrate_target, and burst_guard thresholds.
[02:40] Jonas: continuous_batch_window — this controls how long the scheduler waits to accumulate tokens for a batch; longer windows raise throughput but increase p50/p90 latency. given your bursts, we recommended adaptive windows where window shrinks when queue depth low and expands during sustained high RPS.
[02:58] Aisha: are we able to do adaptive windows with our on-prem control plane? we want deterministic behavior during trading hours.
[03:10] Jonas: yes, the runtime supports a rule-based governor. you can pin windows per time-of-day or use auto-mode. rule-based means you can enforce a hard max latency during trading hours (e.g., 200ms). auto-mode tries to optimize throughput subject to latency SLO.
[03:29] Luca: how does max_num_seqs interact — is it absolute per GPU or per model instance?
[03:40] Jonas: it's per-worker (per-GPU process). if you raise max_num_seqs you increase concurrency but reduce per-sequence compute budget and can push memory pressure — causing more KV thrashing. for long sequences, lowering max_num_seqs and increasing batch time is usually better.
[04:05] Aisha: we have lots of mixed workloads. sometimes a short query hits and then a long summary starts, how do we avoid short queries waiting too long?
[04:18] Jonas: that's token-floor and priority windows. you can set a token_floor so short queries below X tokens are served in a low-latency fast-path with smaller batch target. and priority_windows give a small proportion of slots exclusively for low-token requests.
[04:41] Marco: what about token guards? last time we saw runaway long requests gobble tokens and starve others.
[04:54] Jonas: token guards (per-request token_ceil) prevent a request from consuming unlimited tokens. we also have a soft preempt where after N tokens we can fall back to a lower-cost model or return an early summary. it's pluggable in the policy.

[05:18] Aisha: curious about KV prewarm — we saw cold-cache spikes in previous tests. what patterns reduce cold-cache misses?
[05:30] Jonas: two levers: prefetch_window (the amount of future steps you prefetch into KV) and proactive prewarm where you seed KV with common prefixes during idle time. prefetch_window trades memory for hit-rate. with int8 int4 models, KV size shrinks but hit-rate patterns can remain.
[05:51] Luca: any heuristics for prefetch_window size? we can't just set huge windows due to mem limits.
[06:04] Jonas: start with a window equal to your 95th percentile sequence length, then tune down if memory pressure. for example if p95 seq length = 300 tokens, prefetch_window = 300 gives high hit-rate for subsequent steps. but if you have many concurrent sequences, that becomes heavy. so pair prefetch_window with max_num_seqs constraint.
[06:25] Priya: from security stance, we need to know what prewarming does to data residency — are we copying customer inputs into local KV which persists?
[06:37] Ruth: good call. Redwood on-prem keeps KV in ephemeral RAM per worker and we do not persist user content; KV entries are tied to request prefixes and evicted on policy. we'll provide our on-prem dataflow doc.

[06:55] Jonas: demo time — i have a couple of charts. (brief pause) so here's a test we ran with mixed traffic: baseline (max_num_seqs=128, window=10ms) versus tuned (max_num_seqs=64, window adaptive 5-60ms, token_floor=64, prefetch_window=250). tuned profile increased realized throughput by ~28% while keeping p95 latency within 350ms. baseline hit p95 > 600ms during bursts.
[07:33] Aisha: that p95 improvement is interesting. did you hold model size constant?
[07:39] Jonas: yes same model, v1.3 quantized int8. int4 run had lower memory but p95 had spikes for long sequences due to kernel variance.
[07:52] Luca: can we simulate our exact burst shape? we prefer to run burdened simulation because our bursts are short.
[08:01] Maya: absolutely, our pilot plan is to replay your histograms against a staging on-prem cluster. we request two weeks of traffic histograms and sample payloads.

[08:20] Jonas: some gotchas — continuous batching with tiny windows can cause high scheduling overhead. there's a sweet spot where window is big enough to amortize kernel setup but small enough to meet latency SLOs. and avoid oscillation: if the adaptive policy expands and then contracts rapidly you'll see jitter; we throttle adjustment frequency.
[08:42] Marco: how do we set burst_guard?
[08:45] Jonas: burst_guard is a token bucket that limits instantaneous sequence admission. set burst_guard to 2-3x your steady-state max_num_seqs to allow spikes but not collapse the KV cache. pairing burst_guard with fast-eviction thresholds helps.

[09:05] Aisha: let's talk about slot_size — I think you mentioned slots measured in tokens?
[09:11] Jonas: slot_size is the quantum we pack sequences into for a micro-batch. smaller slot_size reduces waste for short queries but increases ops. a typical config: slot_size=32 tokens for chatty workloads; slot_size=128 for long-seq summarization.
[09:29] Luca: any experience with hybrid packing? like prefer prefix packing for short queries then fallback for longs?
[09:36] Jonas: yes hybrid-packing helps. prefer packing for sequences sharing prefixes or similar lengths. fallback is needed when length skew is high. our runtime supports heuristic: pack by length buckets and allow a small slack to include mixed lengths.

[09:55] Priya: on KMS — we will use our internal HSM. what do we need from Redwood?
[10:02] Ruth: for on-prem we support customer-managed KMS integration. we'll need an admin service account and a list of allowed endpoints. Ruth will follow up with the network/KMS integration checklist.

[10:20] Jonas: another note on quantization — with int4 you can fit more sequences and reduce GPU memory footprint which lets you raise max_num_seqs, but kernel variance is model-dependent. for finance models with longer contexts, int8 is safer for p95 tail.

[10:40] Aisha: if we choose int8 and want to increase concurrency, what's the recommended path?
[10:46] Jonas: raise max_num_seqs in small increments, run benchmark with representative mix; monitor KV hit-rate, GPU memory, and p95 latency. also tune prefetch_window down if memory becomes tight. the knob spreadsheet we'll send has recommended starting points per GPU family and model size.

[11:05] Marco: about eviction_policy — LRU vs frequency-based?
[11:11] Jonas: LRU is simple and often good. frequency-based with hot-key tracking works better when you have very skewed key access (e.g., small set of frequently accessed prompts). frequency-based uses a small overhead but improves hit-rate when there are hot prefixes.

[11:27] Luca: what's the operational signal we should monitor?
[11:31] Jonas: key signals: KV hit-rate, prefetch memory usage, scheduler queue depth, batch sizes over time, GPU utilization, p50/p95/p99 latency, and kernel invocation variance. alert thresholds: p95 > SLO, KV hit-rate drop > 10% sudden, or GPU mem usage > 85% for 2+ minutes.

[11:54] Aisha: any plug-and-play configs for trading vs analytics windows?
[11:59] Jonas: we can provide two profile recipes: trading-profile (strict latency SLO, token_floor small, adaptive window with hard max 20ms, reserved fast-path slots) and analytics-profile (higher throughput, large window, prefetch aggressive). toggle by time-of-day or endpoint.

[12:18] Priya: security question — do any of these knobs cause data to be written to disk or logs with user content?
[12:25] Ruth: knobs only affect in-memory behavior. we do have optional audit logs but those can be redacted; default on-prem audit excludes user content. we'll share config options.

[12:40] Jonas: live tuning approach for pilot: step 0 - baseline run w/ conservative knobs; step 1 - run targeted knob changes (max_num_seqs -, prefetch_window +-); step 2 - run stress with your exact burst histograms; step 3 - finalize profile and schedule canary rollout. each step we collect KV hit-rate, batch histograms, and latency tail.

[13:10] Aisha: how long for each step?
[13:13] Jonas: baseline and targeted knob changes can be done in a few hours each; stress run we recommend at least 2 hours to see transient caching behavior. whole pilot about 1 day on a staging cluster.

[13:28] Maya: quick recap before we open for Qs — agreed to share spreadsheet, histograms, network/KMS checklist; schedule pilot; security follow-up. anything else?
[13:40] Marco: we want a pre-run checklist for node sizing — should that be included in the spreadsheet?
[13:46] Jonas: yes we'll add recommended node/pool sizing per profile.

[13:55] Q&A and clarifications:
[13:55] Aisha: on the priority windows you mentioned earlier, what's the ratio you'd suggest for reserved low-latency slots?
[14:05] Jonas: for mixed workloads start with 10-15% of slots reserved for low-token fast-path, tune up if you see short query latencies exceed SLO.
[14:15] Luca: if we see oscillation in adaptive window, can you lock to a rule-based schedule?
[14:20] Jonas: yes completely. you can lock to time-based windows or percentiles, hybrid approach works.

[14:31] Priya: also please provide an architecture diagram that shows where the KMS calls happen during prewarm so we can run a security review.
[14:38] Ruth: will do, we'll annotate the flow with KMS handshake and audit points.

[14:50] Final recap (last 3 minutes):
[14:50] Maya: quick bullets — Jonas spreadsheet by Friday (2026-12-04), Aisha histograms by Monday (2026-12-06), Ruth to send KMS/network checklist by Thursday (2026-12-03), Maya books pilot (target 2026-12-10).
[15:10] Aisha: sounds good, thanks. excited to see the knob matrix.
[15:15] Jonas: thanks all. we'll keep notes on the pilot run plan and include rollback/flakey-run mitigations.
[15:22] Meeting ends.
